title: The Lower East Side

segments.voice: Yesterday, Emma Lazarus, and your line: the new colossus. Did you get the chance to welcome someone standing in a doorway? Today, past the statue and the inspection halls, to the streets where newcomers went next. Day nine hundred ninety-three.

Five flights of narrow stairs. At the top, a small apartment: a kitchen, a front room, and a dark room in between with no window at all. In the front room a sewing machine is already running before sunrise, because the family is paid by the piece. A boarder sleeps on two chairs pushed together. Down in the street, pushcarts sell herring, pickles, pots and eyeglasses. And a few blocks away, tonight, a theater will fill with people laughing and weeping in Yiddish. Today's word is the neighborhood: The Lower East Side.
screen: `FIVE FLIGHTS UP.` → `A SEWING MACHINE BEFORE SUNRISE.` → `PUSHCARTS AND A YIDDISH THEATER.`

segments.voice: The Lower East Side is a neighborhood in Manhattan, and for the Jewish families of the great wave it was often the first address in America, shared with Italian, Irish and other immigrant neighbors. Start with the tenements. These were apartment buildings packed tight, room after room, with little light or air. Toilets were in the hall or the yard. Families took in boarders to make the rent. Over time, reformers pushed for laws that required windows, light and better plumbing, because the buildings themselves were making people sick. Then the work. A great deal of it was in the garment trade: cutting, sewing, pressing, in small crowded shops called sweatshops, or at the kitchen table, paid by the piece. Long days, low pay, and the boss could always find someone newer and hungrier. And yet the same streets were full of life. Yiddish newspapers, with letters from readers asking for advice about love, work and faith. Synagogues in storefronts and in grand buildings. Cafés full of arguments. And the Yiddish theater, where tired workers paid a little to watch family dramas, comedies, and even Shakespeare in Yiddish, and wept openly in their seats. A psalm holds up the picture these families were working toward: "When thou eatest the labour of thy hands, happy shalt thou be, and it shall be well with thee." Not riches. Just eating from your own work, and having it be enough. In the tenements, the labor was brutal and the bread was thin. But people kept singing, praying and going to the theater, and their children climbed down those five flights to school.
screen: `THE TENEMENTS.` · `PAID BY THE PIECE.` · `NEWSPAPERS, SYNAGOGUES, THEATER.` · `THE WORK OF YOUR HANDS.` · then, large: `HAPPY SHALT THOU BE.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: see someone's hard work. Sit comfortably and let your breath settle. Look at one thing near you: your shirt, your chair, the food you'll eat today. Follow it back. Someone sewed it, built it, picked it, packed it, drove it. Let one of those unseen workers become real in your mind: tired hands, a long shift, a family at home. Hold them for a few breaths with respect. Then think of one person you see every day whose work is easy to overlook. Today, thank them by name. The bell holds the time.
Pushcarts. The carts that filled the streets of the Lower East Side, selling herring, pickles, pots and eyeglasses right outside the tenements. Today's word.
Your line: the tenements. Today, when you climb your own stairs or open your own door, give one thought to everyone who had less room and still made a life. Day nine hundred ninety-three.

howItsDone: Jewish families, museums and synagogues on the Lower East Side keep the tenement stories, and Psalm 128 is sung or read in Jewish life, including in some communities at weddings.
